meta.title: Nokia Corporation — Justin Hotard's network-infrastructure pivot through the AI data centre routing opportunity
meta.abstract: Nokia Corporation is a Finnish multinational telecommunications, information technology, and consumer electronics company listed on the Helsinki Stock Exchange (NOKIA) and as American Depositary Receipts on the NYSE under the ticker NOK. Headquartered in Espoo, Finland, Nokia operates four reporting business groups: Network Infrastructure (IP Networks, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, Submarine Networks), Mobile Networks (5G radio access network equipment, broader mobile infrastructure), Cloud and Network Services (broader software and services), and Nokia Technologies (the patent licensing business). The corporate trajectory through 2016-2026 has been substantially shaped by the January 2016 Alcatel-Lucent acquisition (closed for approximately EUR 15.6 billion in shares creating the combined Nokia-Alcatel-Lucent organisation), the multi-year operational and strategic posture refinement under successive CEOs (Rajeev Suri 2014-2020, Pekka Lundmark August 2020-March 2025, Justin Hotard April 2025-present), and more recent strategic positioning toward AI data centre opportunity through the Network Infrastructure business group particularly the IP Networks routing portfolio. Hotard joined Nokia from Intel Corporation where he had been Executive Vice President and General Manager of Data Center and AI Group; the CEO mandate has been the AI data centre opportunity development through the Network Infrastructure business group plus the broader operational and strategic posture continuation. Fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately EUR 19.7 billion reflecting the broader business group trajectory.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Nokia Corporation — headquartered in Espoo, Finland, listed on Nasdaq Helsinki under `NOKIA` and trading in the US under `NOK` — entered 2025 at a genuine strategic hinge point. On 28 February 2025 it completed the acquisition of [Infinera Corporation](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/), a transaction Nokia had announced in June 2024 at an enterprise value of roughly $2.3 billion. Just over a month later, on 1 April 2025, Justin Hotard succeeded Pekka Lundmark as President and Chief Executive Officer. Those two moves — one portfolio-expanding, one managerial — turned a company still identified by many investors with 5G radio access into one that was explicitly trying to sell optical, routing and software infrastructure into the AI build-out. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/) [Nokia Infinera close](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/)

By the frozen snapshot date, that repositioning had moved beyond rhetoric but not yet into maturity. Nokia's Q1 2026 disclosures showed AI & Cloud net sales up 49 per cent year on year and representing 8 per cent of group sales for the quarter, while Network Infrastructure grew 6 per cent and Optical Networks 20 per cent. The direction was clear; the scale remained early relative to the size of the overall company. [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

## The Succession and Its Rationale

Hotard's appointment was unusually explicit in strategic intent. Nokia's own transition release described him as a US national born in 1974, with more than 25 years in global technology companies, then serving as Executive Vice President and General Manager of Intel's Data Center & AI Group. Before Intel, he spent almost a decade at Hewlett Packard Enterprise, including as Executive Vice President and General Manager of High Performance Computing, AI & Labs. His formal education was a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and an MBA from MIT Sloan. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

Sari Baldauf, then chair of Nokia's board, framed the hire in the terms that mattered to investors:

> "He has a strong track record of accelerating growth in technology companies along with vast expertise in AI and data center markets."

Hotard's own opening statement made the same point less diplomatically:

> "Networks are the backbone that power society and businesses, and enable generational technology shifts like the one we are currently experiencing in AI."

[Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

His first shareholder letter, in the Q1 2025 interim report, was not a manifesto so much as a capital-allocation brief. He said his early focus was to drive efficiency while investing "in the right growth segments", and he singled out hyperscale, enterprise and defence as areas where Nokia could expand. That phrasing mattered because it put the burden of proof on the non-carrier parts of the portfolio almost immediately. [Nokia Q1 2025 interim report](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/04/24/nokia-corporation-interim-report-for-q1-2025/)

## Four Business Groups, Then Two Operating Segments

When Hotard took office, Nokia still reported through four business groups. Network Infrastructure, then led by Federico Guillén, housed IP Networks, Optical Networks and Fixed Networks. Mobile Networks remained under Tommi Uitto. Cloud and Network Services was led by Raghav Sahgal. Nokia Technologies, which monetised the patent estate, had already passed from Jenni Lukander to Patrik Hammarén on 22 January 2025. [Patrik Hammarén appointment](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/patrik-hammaren-appointed-as-president-of-nokia-technologies/) [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

That structure did not last. On 19 November 2025, at its capital markets day, Nokia said it would simplify into two primary operating segments — Network Infrastructure and Mobile Infrastructure — from 1 January 2026. The company paired the structural change with a long-term target of EUR 2.7 billion to EUR 3.2 billion of comparable operating profit by 2028 and strategic KPIs that included 6-8 per cent annual net-sales growth for Network Infrastructure and 10-12 per cent growth for the combined Optical Networks and IP Networks franchises. Under the same reset, Hotard took Mobile Infrastructure on an interim basis, Sahgal moved to Chief Customer Officer, and Hammarén remained in the leadership team as President of Technology Standards, the unit that absorbed the former Nokia Technologies reporting line. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/) [Nokia strategy summary](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-unveils-strategy-to-capture-value-from-ai-supercycle/)

## Revenue Backdrop

The revenue context was weaker than the strategic language. Nokia's reported continuing-operations net sales had peaked at EUR 23.761 billion in 2022, fallen to EUR 21.138 billion in 2023 and then to EUR 19.220 billion in 2024, before recovering modestly to EUR 19.889 billion in 2025. The 2024 and 2025 figures were reported after the Submarine Networks business had been carved out as a discontinued operation, and Nokia's own annual report recast the comparative years accordingly. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

| Year | Net sales, continuing operations (EUR bn) |
|---|---|
| 2020 | 21.852 |
| 2021 | 22.202 |
| 2022 | 23.761 |
| 2023 | 21.138 |
| 2024 | 19.220 |
| 2025 | 19.889 |

The more current signal by the frozen date came from Q1 2026. Nokia reported EUR 4.5 billion of net sales, a gross margin of 45.5 per cent, an operating margin of 6.2 per cent, free cash flow of EUR 0.6 billion and net cash of EUR 3.8 billion. Network Infrastructure grew 6 per cent, Optical Networks 20 per cent, while AI & Cloud orders reached EUR 1.0 billion in the quarter. [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

## Infinera Integration and Optical Scale

Infinera was the most consequential portfolio change of the Hotard period's opening phase because it changed the optical business from a capable subscale unit into one Nokia could market as an AI-era backbone. Nokia's Q1 2025 slides said the combined optical franchise would have held 26 per cent pro forma market share in 2024, excluding China and excluding SLTE and Nokia ASN, and reiterated a target of EUR 200 million of operating-profit synergies by 2027. In the first full quarter after closing, Optical Networks grew 15 per cent. In Q4 2025 it grew 17 per cent, and in Q1 2026 it accelerated again to 20 per cent. [Nokia Q1 2025 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2025-04/nokia_slides_2025_q1_fi.pdf) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

The operational content of those numbers was also more concrete than the earlier draft suggested. Nokia repeatedly said order intake in optical and IP remained above one, driven by AI & Cloud customers, and management's 2026 guidance explicitly contemplated higher capital expenditure to expand optical manufacturing capacity. This was not a theoretical adjacency by spring 2026; it was already influencing factory planning and capital deployment. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## IP Networks, Hyperscalers and the NVIDIA Signal

The routing side of the thesis had also moved from aspiration to early commercial proof points. In late 2024 Nokia announced an IP network build for [Nscale](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-building-ip-network-to-support-ai-workloads-at-nscales-new-sustainable-data-center/)'s AI-focused data centre in Stavanger, and in May 2025 it disclosed a routing-based network-edge deployment for [CoreSite](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/05/13/nokia-selected-by-coresite-for-routing-based-network-edge-solution-to-support-data-intensive-mission-critical-applications/) across 30 US data centres in 11 markets. By September 2025 Nokia and [Supermicro](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-supermicro-partner-to-deliver-integrated-ai-optimized-data-center-networking-solutions/) had announced a joint AI-optimised data-centre networking solution built around SR Linux and Nokia's Event-Driven Automation platform. These were still footholds, not franchise-defining volumes, but they were real disclosed deployments rather than generic management aspiration.

The sharpest external endorsement arrived on 28 October 2025, when Nokia said its board had approved a directed share issue for 166,389,351 new shares to enable NVIDIA to make a USD 1.0 billion equity investment at USD 6.01 per share, alongside a strategic partnership around AI-RAN and 6G. By March 2026 Nokia was saying it had 10 publicly committed AI-RAN customers and remained on track to begin customer trials later in the year. [NVIDIA investment release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nvidia-to-make-usd-1-billion-equity-investment-in-nokia-in-addition-to-new-strategic-partnership-nokias-board-resolved-on-directed-share-issuance-to-nvidia/) [Nokia AI-RAN update](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2026/03/01/nokia-accelerates-ai-ran-momentum-with-new-partnerships-driving-path-to-ai-native-6g-mwc26/) [NVIDIA and Nokia partnership](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nvidia-and-nokia-to-pioneer-the-ai-platform-for-6g--powering-americas-return-to-telecommunications-leadership/)

## Open Questions

By 23 May 2026, the dossier's core questions had narrowed rather than disappeared. Nokia had clearly found a more attractive demand pocket in AI & Cloud, but that business still accounted for only 8 per cent of Q1 2026 sales. Network Infrastructure was growing, and management said it expected 12-14 per cent growth for the full year, yet the group still depended on a much larger mobile business whose recovery was described as stable rather than robust. The NVIDIA partnership and the Infinera integration had improved Nokia's strategic optics. The unresolved issue was whether those moves would translate into a durable rerating of the income statement rather than a series of promising, but still comparatively small, wins. [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

chapters.title: From 1865 Finnish founding through Alcatel-Lucent, Lundmark, Infinera, and Hotard
chapters.body:
## The Finnish Conglomerate, 1865–1990

Nokia Corporation's origins bear almost no resemblance to the telecommunications equipment vendor it became. On 12 May 1865, a Finnish mining engineer named Fredrik Idestam established a wood-pulp mill on the banks of the Tammerkoski rapids near Tampere. A second mill followed on the Nokianvirta river, and the company formally adopted the Nokia name in 1871. For most of the nineteenth century, its business was paper. [Nokia history](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/our-history/)

The twentieth century transformed it into something more complex. A series of mergers across rubber manufacturing — Finnish Rubber Works joined the group in 1922 — and cable production — Finnish Cable Works in 1967 — produced a diversified industrial conglomerate operating across tyres, consumer footwear, consumer electronics, and telecommunications cables. The three-company structure formalised as Nokia Corporation in 1967. By the 1980s the group had moved into mobile telecommunications in earnest, supplying analogue network equipment and, from 1987, handsets for the Nordic Mobile Telephone standard. Finland's cold, dispersed geography provided the demand logic. Nokia was a conglomerate learning, improbably, to become a technology company.

## The Mobile Phone Era and Its End

The 1990s produced the most dramatic transformation in Nokia's history. The company divested its non-core industrial businesses — rubber, cables, consumer electronics — and concentrated almost entirely on mobile handsets and network infrastructure. The timing proved extraordinarily fortunate. Global mobile adoption accelerated through the decade, and by the early 2000s Nokia had become the world's largest handset maker and one of Europe's most valuable listed companies. [Nokia history](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/our-history/)

The collapse arrived with the iPhone. Apple's entry into smartphones in 2007, followed by Google's Android platform in 2008, exposed Nokia's Symbian software stack as inadequate for the new computing paradigm. Nokia's response — the Symbian defence, the belated Microsoft Windows Phone partnership announced in February 2011 under incoming CEO Stephen Elop — failed to arrest the decline. Market share collapsed from above forty percent to single digits within five years. The handset business that had defined the company for two decades became unsustainable.

In September 2013, Nokia's board agreed to sell the Devices and Services division to Microsoft Corporation for €5.44 billion. The transaction completed on 25 April 2014. What remained was a smaller, structurally different entity: Nokia Solutions and Networks, the telecommunications infrastructure business, plus Nokia Technologies, the patent licensing operation. The handset era was over. The network infrastructure era was beginning. [Microsoft close](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-sale-of-substantially-all-of-its-devices--services-business-to-microsoft/)

## The Alcatel-Lucent Acquisition, January 2016

The strategic direction clarified in April 2015, when Nokia announced an agreement to acquire Alcatel-Lucent, the Franco-American telecommunications equipment vendor that carried the heritage of AT&T's Bell Laboratories. Nokia valued the transaction at approximately €15.6 billion, and combined operations began on 14 January 2016. [Nokia and Alcatel-Lucent to combine](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2015/04/15/nokia-and-alcatel-lucent-to-combine-to-create-an-innovation-leader-in-next-generation-technology-and-services-for-an-ip-connected-world/) [First day of combined operations](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-celebrates-first-day-of-combined-operations-with-alcatel-lucent/)

The Alcatel-Lucent acquisition brought three capabilities that would prove foundational to the subsequent decade. First, it delivered IP Networks routing — specifically the 7750 Service Router platform and the broader IP/MPLS networking portfolio — which established Nokia in carrier routing alongside Cisco and Juniper. Second, it added a coherent optical transport portfolio through Alcatel-Lucent's Wavelength Division Multiplexing business. Third, it transferred the Bell Laboratories research lineage and the accompanying US government, enterprise, and hyperscaler customer relationships that Alcatel-Lucent had cultivated across decades. Nokia paid a substantial premium for a struggling asset; it acquired capabilities whose strategic value would compound across the following decade in ways not immediately apparent at close.

CEO Rajeev Suri, who led Nokia from 2014 through 2020, oversaw the integration and used the enlarged platform to position Nokia as a primary 5G infrastructure vendor. On Nokia's later recast continuing-operations basis, the 5G cycle produced a revenue expansion that peaked at EUR 23.761 billion in 2022 before a sharp deceleration as carrier capital expenditure moderated globally. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/)

## The Lundmark Era: 2020–2025

Pekka Lundmark succeeded Suri as chief executive in August 2020, inheriting a company that had grown rapidly but whose cost structure had not kept pace with the strategic transformation. Lundmark, a Finnish engineer who had previously run Fortum, the state-controlled energy company, and earlier held senior roles at Nokia and Kone, moved quickly to restructure.

The Lundmark programme had three principal dimensions. Organisational simplification first: Nokia consolidated around four business groups — Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, and Nokia Technologies — creating clearer profit-and-loss accountability. Cost reduction second: Nokia first pursued an earlier savings programme and later, in the 2024-2026 restructuring phase, targeted a gross cost-base reduction of EUR 800 million to EUR 1.2 billion versus 2023. Strategic repositioning third: Lundmark consistently framed Nokia as a network infrastructure pure-play, differentiating it from Ericsson's mobile-heavy mix and from Cisco's software-heavy positioning. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

Revenue through the Lundmark period fell from the EUR 23.761 billion 2022 peak to EUR 19.220 billion in 2024 on Nokia's continuing-operations basis as carrier spending softened — a trajectory detailed in the Snapshot chapter. The compression concentrated strategic attention on Network Infrastructure, where the Alcatel-Lucent-inherited IP routing and optical transport capabilities offered structural diversification away from mobile carrier spending cycles. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/)

## The Infinera Acquisition, 2024–2025

In June 2024, Nokia announced the acquisition of Infinera Corporation, a US-based optical transport equipment vendor listed on Nasdaq, in a transaction valued at roughly $2.3 billion on an enterprise-value basis. The strategic logic was explicit and multi-dimensional. [Nokia to acquire Infinera](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-to-acquire-infinera-to-increase-scale-in-optical-networks-and-accelerate-product-roadmap/)

Infinera contributed a coherent optical transport product line anchored by the ICE (Infinite Capacity Engine) digital signal processor chipset, which had earned a position among hyperscaler and data centre interconnect customers seeking high-capacity, programmable optical transport. Critically, Infinera brought a US-anchored customer base that skewed toward technology companies, cloud providers, and Latin American carriers — categories that complemented Nokia's existing telecommunications relationships and provided exposure to hyperscaler capital expenditure cycles increasingly dominated by AI infrastructure deployment. The acquisition also provided US manufacturing presence and US-based engineering design capability relevant to evolving supply chain requirements and the increasing sensitivity of US government and enterprise customers to vendor provenance.

The transaction received regulatory approvals and closed on 28 February 2025. The combined Optical Networks segment — incorporating the legacy Nokia portfolio and the Infinera assets — emerged as a substantially larger participant in data-centre interconnect and long-haul optical infrastructure, positioned precisely as hyperscaler spending on AI training and inference clusters was accelerating demand for high-bandwidth optical connectivity between facilities. [Nokia Infinera close](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/)

## The Hotard Succession, April 2025

Justin Hotard assumed the presidency and chief executive role on 1 April 2025, succeeding Lundmark. The board's selection telegraphed a strategic direction the company had been building toward since the Alcatel-Lucent integration: Nokia's routing and optical assets had begun to gain traction in AI and cloud infrastructure, and Hotard's Intel and HPE background positioned him to accelerate that pivot. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

The company that began as a paper mill on the Nokia River in 1865, that briefly led the world in mobile handsets, and that acquired the Bell Laboratories heritage in January 2016, was entering its latest strategic chapter under its newest chief executive: a European-listed network infrastructure vendor with American leadership, seeking to position Alcatel-Lucent's inherited routing capability and Infinera's freshly integrated optical transport assets at the centre of the most capital-intensive infrastructure build-out of the AI era.

chapters.title: Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, Nokia Technologies
chapters.body:
## Four Groups, Then an Operating Model Reset

Nokia entered 2025 still reporting through four business groups — Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, and Nokia Technologies. By the frozen snapshot date, however, that structure was already in the past tense. At its 19 November 2025 capital markets day, Nokia said it would simplify into two primary operating segments from 1 January 2026: Network Infrastructure and Mobile Infrastructure. The latter folded together Core Software, Radio Networks and Technology Standards, the unit that replaced the former Nokia Technologies reporting line. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/) [Nokia strategy summary](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-unveils-strategy-to-capture-value-from-ai-supercycle/)

That reorganisation mattered because it clarified which parts of Nokia were meant to grow and which were meant to fund the transition. Through 2025, the group's legacy shape remained visible in the accounts; by 2026, management was presenting the portfolio much more bluntly as a Network Infrastructure growth story and a Mobile Infrastructure cash-and-technology base. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Network Infrastructure: The Growth Engine

Network Infrastructure was not Nokia's largest 2024 business group by revenue — Mobile Networks remained larger — but it was the portfolio most central to Hotard's thesis. In 2024 Network Infrastructure generated EUR 6.518 billion of net sales, comprising EUR 2.583 billion from IP Networks, EUR 1.636 billion from Optical Networks and EUR 2.299 billion from Fixed Networks. Nokia's Q4 2024 report simultaneously committed up to EUR 100 million of additional annual operating expenditure to pursue EUR 1 billion of incremental data-centre-networking net sales by 2028, making the investment agenda explicit rather than inferred. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

### IP Networks

IP Networks sat at the centre of the AI narrative. The business traced to Alcatel-Lucent's service-router heritage, but Nokia was selling it into a different buyer set. The flagship story by late 2024 was not just carrier core routing; it was SR Linux and the 7250 IXR family as a data-centre fabric platform. Nokia's public disclosures showed concrete wins with AI-linked customers rather than generic aspiration: [Nscale](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-building-ip-network-to-support-ai-workloads-at-nscales-new-sustainable-data-center/) selected Nokia in December 2024 for its new AI data centre in Stavanger; [CoreSite](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/05/13/nokia-selected-by-coresite-for-routing-based-network-edge-solution-to-support-data-intensive-mission-critical-applications/) chose Nokia in May 2025 for an IP-routing edge-and-core solution across 30 US data centres in 11 markets; and Nokia used its Q4 2025 results to say order intake in both optical and IP remained above one, driven by AI & Cloud customers. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

Nokia's own long-term KPIs reinforced where management believed the upside sat. At the November 2025 capital markets day the company targeted 10-12 per cent annual growth for the combined Optical Networks and IP Networks franchises through 2028. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

### Optical Networks

Optical Networks was the business most visibly transformed by Infinera. Nokia's Q1 2025 slides said the pro forma combination would have carried 26 per cent market share in 2024, excluding China and excluding SLTE and Nokia ASN, and reaffirmed a EUR 200 million operating-profit-synergy target by 2027. The business then posted a sequence of growth figures that made the integration story tangible: +15 per cent in Q1 2025, +17 per cent in Q4 2025 and +20 per cent in Q1 2026, all on Nokia's constant-currency, comparable basis. [Nokia Q1 2025 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2025-04/nokia_slides_2025_q1_fi.pdf) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

The strategic logic was straightforward. Infinera contributed coherent optical technology, US manufacturing and engineering depth, and customer exposure to hyperscalers and North American cloud interconnect spending that Nokia had not built to the same degree organically. By the frozen window, Optical Networks had become the fastest-growing major sub-business in the company. [Nokia Infinera close](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/)

### Fixed Networks

Fixed Networks remained a substantial but less fashionable part of the portfolio. In 2024 it generated EUR 2.299 billion of net sales. Nokia's positioning there centred on fibre access, PON and broadband platforms rather than the AI narrative that dominated Hotard's public messaging. The portfolio was also narrowing by the frozen date: on 30 April 2026 Nokia announced that [Inseego would acquire Nokia's Fixed Wireless Access business](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inseego-to-acquire-nokias-fixed-wireless-access-business-to-create-a-global-wireless-broadband-leader/), leaving Fixed Networks more concentrated around fibre access and related software. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

## Mobile Networks, Then Mobile Infrastructure

Mobile Networks remained the larger revenue base through 2025. The business generated EUR 7.725 billion of net sales in 2024 and, according to Nokia's Q4 2025 report, was flat for full-year 2025 while growing 6 per cent in Q4. The shift in terminology after 1 January 2026 was not cosmetic. Mobile Infrastructure bundled core software, radio networks and technology standards under a single leader — Hotard on an interim basis — and was designed to sharpen accountability around profitability and 6G-era technology leadership rather than simple top-line expansion. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/) [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

The public contract trail supported Nokia's claim to remain relevant in radio. Representative disclosed wins before the frozen date included the October 2022 multi-year [Reliance Jio](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2022/10/17/nokia-wins-multi-year-deal-with-reliance-jio-india-to-build-one-of-the-largest-5g-networks-in-the-world/) supply agreement for one of the world's largest 5G roll-outs, the November 2025 [Telefónica Germany](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-telefonica-germany-agree-5-year-ran-deal-to-advance-5g-expansion/) extension for 5G RAN, and the March 2026 [Virgin Media O2](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-wins-new-5g-ran-deal-with-virgin-media-o2-to-accelerate-its-mobile-transformation-plan/) multi-year 5G deployment and modernisation programme in the UK.

| Representative disclosed mobile-network contracts | Date | What Nokia disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| Reliance Jio | 17 Oct 2022 | Multi-year 5G RAN supply agreement across India |
| Telefónica Germany | 26 Nov 2025 | Five-year extension for 5G RAN network |
| Virgin Media O2 | 31 Mar 2026 | New multi-year 5G RAN deployment and modernisation programme |

Those disclosures did not prove share leadership, but they did support the narrower claim that Nokia remained embedded in large-scale RAN programmes across India, Germany and the UK.

## Cloud and Network Services

Cloud and Network Services generated EUR 3.022 billion of net sales in 2024. It was the smallest of the four legacy business groups, but it mattered because it pulled more software and services into the mix and because parts of it later migrated into the 2026 Mobile Infrastructure structure. Nokia's cost programme also made clear that CNS would bear a material share of the restructuring burden: the company said roughly 30 per cent of the expected savings from its 2024-2026 cost programme would come from Cloud and Network Services. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

The commercial positioning before the frozen date focused on carrier-core software, automation and private-network software rather than consumer-facing applications. In Q1 2025 Nokia said Cloud and Network Services grew 8 per cent, driven by 5G-core demand, and by the November 2025 operating-model reset Sahgal was being moved out of a stand-alone CNS presidency into the broader role of Chief Customer Officer. [Nokia Q1 2025 interim report](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/04/24/nokia-corporation-interim-report-for-q1-2025/) [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

## Nokia Technologies, Then Technology Standards

Nokia Technologies was the outlier in the portfolio because its economics were licensing economics rather than equipment economics. In February 2024 Nokia said it had concluded its smartphone patent-renewal cycle, had signed its seventh major smartphone agreement in thirteen months, and now had a contracted annual net-sales run-rate of approximately EUR 1.3 billion, excluding catch-up payments, with a mid-term run-rate target of EUR 1.4 billion to EUR 1.5 billion. The catch-up payments then drove 2024 net sales in the unit to EUR 1.928 billion. By Q4 2025 Nokia said the contracted run-rate remained EUR 1.4 billion. [Nokia smartphone renewal cycle](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-concludes-smartphone-patent-license-renewal-cycle/) [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

Leadership also changed earlier than the draft reflected. Patrik Hammarén was appointed President of Nokia Technologies on 22 January 2025, and from 1 January 2026 he remained in Nokia's leadership team as President of Technology Standards. [Patrik Hammarén appointment](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/patrik-hammaren-appointed-as-president-of-nokia-technologies/) [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

## Segment Structure in Context

| Legacy 2024 business group | Net sales (EUR bn) | What it represented by the frozen window |
|---|---|---|
| Network Infrastructure | 6.518 | The clearest growth platform, especially in optical and AI-linked IP networking |
| Mobile Networks | 7.725 | The larger but lower-growth revenue base that was recast into Mobile Infrastructure |
| Cloud and Network Services | 3.022 | Software, services and core-network capabilities later folded into the 2026 model |
| Nokia Technologies | 1.928 | High-margin licensing stream, later restyled as Technology Standards |

The essential fact was not that Nokia possessed four business groups in 2025. It was that by May 2026 management had already decided that the old structure obscured where value would be created. The company was reorganising around a simpler distinction: Network Infrastructure as the growth vector into AI and cloud, and Mobile Infrastructure as the technology, patent and carrier base from which that growth attempt would be funded. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment economics, capital allocation
chapters.body:
Nokia's recent financial history is easier to read once the accounting basis is cleaned up. The most important adjustment is that the Submarine Networks business was classified as a discontinued operation in June 2024, and Nokia recast the comparative numbers accordingly. The properly comparable top-line series for continuing operations was therefore lower than the draft suggested: EUR 21.852 billion in 2020, EUR 22.202 billion in 2021, EUR 23.761 billion in 2022, EUR 21.138 billion in 2023, EUR 19.220 billion in 2024 and EUR 19.889 billion in 2025. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## The Revenue Arc, Corrected

The underlying narrative still held: Nokia rode a 5G and broadband cycle into a 2022 high, then spent two years absorbing a carrier-spending correction before managing a small rebound in 2025. But the scale of that cycle changed once measured on a like-for-like basis. From the EUR 23.761 billion peak in 2022, continuing-operations net sales fell EUR 4.541 billion to EUR 19.220 billion in 2024, a decline of roughly 19 per cent. Full-year 2025 recovered only part of that loss, with reported net sales up 3 per cent to EUR 19.889 billion. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

| Fiscal year | Net sales, continuing operations (EUR bn) | YoY change |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 21.852 | — |
| 2021 | 22.202 | +1.6% |
| 2022 | 23.761 | +7.0% |
| 2023 | 21.138 | -11.0% |
| 2024 | 19.220 | -9.1% |
| 2025 | 19.889 | +3.5% |

That 2025 recovery also looked different beneath the surface. Nokia's Q4 2025 report said full-year comparable net sales rose 2 per cent on a constant-currency, portfolio basis, comparable operating profit came in at EUR 2.0 billion and free cash flow at EUR 1.5 billion, a 72 per cent conversion rate. In other words, 2025 was not a return to the 2022 peak; it was a year in which the business stabilised, re-mixed and funded new growth spending. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Segment Economics

The 2024 business-group mix explained why management became more interested in composition than in simple scale. Mobile Networks remained the largest legacy business group at EUR 7.725 billion of net sales, but Network Infrastructure was not far behind at EUR 6.518 billion. Cloud and Network Services contributed EUR 3.022 billion, while Nokia Technologies generated EUR 1.928 billion, inflated that year by catch-up licensing revenue after the smartphone renewal cycle concluded. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/) [Nokia smartphone renewal cycle](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-concludes-smartphone-patent-license-renewal-cycle/)

By late 2025 management was much more explicit about where it wanted growth to come from. The Q4 2025 report said Network Infrastructure delivered 7 per cent comparable net-sales growth in the quarter, including 17 per cent growth in Optical Networks, and that order intake remained above one across both optical and IP. By contrast, Mobile Networks was flat for full-year 2025 and Nokia Technologies was described in run-rate terms rather than as a top-line growth engine. The economics that mattered most to Hotard were therefore not the economics of the company Nokia had been; they were the economics of the combined optical-and-routing franchise after Infinera. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

Nokia's Q1 2026 disclosures sharpened the same point. Group net sales were EUR 4.5 billion, but AI & Cloud net sales grew 49 per cent and accounted for 8 per cent of the quarter's sales, while Network Infrastructure grew 6 per cent and Optical Networks 20 per cent. Those figures did not yet dominate the group P&L. They did show where the faster-growing mix was coming from. [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

## Margin and R&D Reality

One of the larger factual misses in the draft was research spending. Nokia was not spending 15-17 per cent of sales on R&D in the period immediately before the frozen date. The 2024 annual report put research-and-development expense at EUR 4.512 billion, or 23.5 per cent of net sales. The 2025 financial report then showed reported R&D expense of EUR 4.855 billion, up 8 per cent year on year. Those were unusually heavy research ratios for a company in a down-cycle, but they were also exactly what management said it intended: protect technology leadership, fund the AI-and-cloud push, and accept that near-term margins would absorb the cost. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

The trade-off was visible in profitability. Reported operating profit from continuing operations was EUR 1.711 billion in 2024 and EUR 885 million in 2025, while comparable operating profit fell from EUR 2.584 billion in 2024 to EUR 2.024 billion in 2025 as Nokia invested in Network Infrastructure growth and absorbed Infinera. Hotard and Lundmark were not trying to defend the old margin profile mechanically; they were trying to spend through the transition without breaking the balance sheet. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Capital Structure and Cash

The balance-sheet description in the earlier draft was directionally right but too static. Nokia ended 2024 with free cash flow of EUR 2.0 billion and net cash of EUR 4.9 billion. After the Infinera acquisition and the year of additional Network Infrastructure investment, it ended 2025 with Q4 free cash flow of EUR 0.2 billion, full-year free cash flow of EUR 1.5 billion and net cash of EUR 3.4 billion. By Q1 2026 net cash had risen again to EUR 3.8 billion and quarterly free cash flow to EUR 0.6 billion. That pattern supported management's claim that the company still had financial room to integrate Infinera, invest in optical capacity and maintain shareholder distributions without approaching a stressed capital position. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

The deal itself also had a clearer financing profile than the draft implied. Nokia said when it announced the acquisition in June 2024 that Infinera was valued at an enterprise value of about $2.3 billion, with an equity value of about $1.7 billion, and up to 30 per cent of the consideration could be paid in Nokia ADSs depending on Infinera shareholder elections. That equity component was one reason Nokia simultaneously prepared an anti-dilution buyback programme. [Nokia to acquire Infinera](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-to-acquire-infinera-to-increase-scale-in-optical-networks-and-accelerate-product-roadmap/)

## Cost Savings, But With a Different Endgame

The post-2023 restructuring was also more extensive than the draft's single number suggested. Nokia's 2024-2026 programme targeted a reduction in gross cost base of EUR 800 million to EUR 1.2 billion by the end of 2026 versus 2023, equal to a 10-15 per cent cut in personnel expense and intended to move Nokia toward a 72,000-77,000 employee organisation from 86,000 when the programme was announced. The company said the current plan envisaged roughly EUR 1.0 billion of gross cost savings, though the number remained contingent on demand. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

By January 2026 management was layering a second set of moving parts on top of that programme. The Q4 2025 report introduced 2026 assumptions that included EUR 400 million of recurring gross cost savings, EUR 250 million of restructuring charges and EUR 450 million of associated cash outflows, excluding Infinera-related synergies. The company was therefore simultaneously cutting cost, raising optical capacity and integrating two separate structural changes: Infinera and the internal reporting reset. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Share Repurchase and Capital Return

Nokia's capital return was more concrete than the draft's generic description. In January 2024 the board initiated a share buyback programme to return up to EUR 600 million to shareholders. Nokia later accelerated that programme and completed it on 21 November 2024; the 157,646,220 repurchased shares were cancelled on 4 December 2024. Separately, after agreeing the Infinera acquisition, Nokia launched a second buyback on 22 November 2024 targeting 150 million shares for an aggregate purchase price not exceeding EUR 900 million to offset dilution from the equity component of the deal. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

The dividend policy also remained active. The board proposed a EUR 0.14-per-share distribution in respect of both the 2024 and 2025 financial years, structured as board-authorised instalments rather than a one-shot AGM cash dividend. This was not a company hoarding cash for survival; it was a company willing to distribute cash while still telling investors that additional optical manufacturing capacity, AI & Cloud expansion and Infinera synergies would absorb real capital. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia AGM 2026 resolutions](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/resolutions-of-nokia-corporations-annual-general-meeting-and-board-of-directors-assembly-meeting-807431/)

## What the Model Looked Like by the Frozen Date

By 23 May 2026 the financial model had become easier to describe, even if it was not yet fully proven. Nokia was a EUR 20 billion-revenue company whose carrier businesses had stopped collapsing, whose licensing arm still threw off cash, and whose growth argument now depended on Optical Networks and IP Networks sustaining double-digit expansion inside a broader Network Infrastructure segment. Management's full-year 2026 guide called for EUR 2.0 billion to EUR 2.5 billion of comparable operating profit, while Q1 2026 commentary said performance was tracking somewhat above the midpoint and Network Infrastructure was expected to grow 12-14 per cent for the year. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

That left the essential question unchanged but better framed. Nokia no longer needed to prove merely that it could survive a mobile capex downturn. It needed to prove that the optical-and-routing growth it had bought and then funded could become large enough to change the trajectory of the whole group.

chapters.title: Post-Lundmark era through Infinera close and Hotard succession
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Compression That Forced a Reckoning

The revenue compression was real, but the properly comparable series was smaller than the draft suggested. On Nokia's continuing-operations basis, net sales fell from EUR 23.761 billion in 2022 to EUR 19.220 billion in 2024 before edging back to EUR 19.889 billion in 2025. In parallel, Nokia's 2024-2026 restructuring programme targeted a gross cost-base reduction of EUR 800 million to EUR 1.2 billion versus 2023 and a move toward a 72,000-77,000 employee organisation from 86,000 when the programme was announced. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

## Infinera and the Optical Bet

The Infinera close on 28 February 2025 altered the growth story faster than it altered the group P&L. Nokia said the enlarged optical business would have carried 26 per cent pro forma market share in 2024, excluding China and excluding SLTE and Nokia ASN, and it reaffirmed a EUR 200 million operating-profit-synergy target by 2027. Optical Networks then grew 15 per cent in Q1 2025, 17 per cent in Q4 2025 and 20 per cent in Q1 2026. [Nokia Infinera close](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/) [Nokia Q1 2025 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2025-04/nokia_slides_2025_q1_fi.pdf) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

## The Succession and What It Signalled

Hotard succeeded Lundmark on 1 April 2025, but the strategic signal was broader than one CEO change. Nokia spent the rest of 2025 replacing the leadership of Network Infrastructure with David Heard, absorbing Infinera, simplifying into Network Infrastructure and Mobile Infrastructure from 1 January 2026, and using capital markets day in November 2025 to state openly that AI and cloud were now the centre of the growth agenda. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/) [Group leadership changes, June 2025](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-changes-to-group-leadership-team/) [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)

## Hotard's Cadence

The earnings cadence by the frozen date showed why investors were prepared to follow the argument, but not yet fully underwrite it. Full-year 2025 comparable operating profit came in at EUR 2.0 billion and free cash flow at EUR 1.5 billion. In Q1 2026 Nokia reported AI & Cloud net sales growth of 49 per cent, EUR 1.0 billion of AI & Cloud orders in the quarter, and guidance that Network Infrastructure should grow 12-14 per cent for full-year 2026. The growth engine had become visible; it had not yet become the whole machine. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

chapters.title: Justin Hotard, Marco Wirén CFO, segment leadership, and the Baldauf-chaired board
chapters.body:
## The Succession

On 10 February 2025, Nokia announced the leadership change that defined the dossier's central period. Pekka Lundmark, who had returned in August 2020, would step down as President and CEO on 31 March 2025. Justin Hotard would take over on 1 April 2025, with Lundmark remaining as an adviser through the end of the year to support the transition. The arrangement mattered because it bridged not only a CEO handover but also the immediate post-close integration of Infinera. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

Sari Baldauf, then chair of the board, left no doubt about the logic of the appointment:

> "I am delighted to welcome Justin to Nokia. He has a strong track record of accelerating growth in technology companies along with vast expertise in AI and data center markets, which are critical areas for Nokia's future growth."

Hotard answered in the same register:

> "Networks are the backbone that power society and businesses, and enable generational technology shifts like the one we are currently experiencing in AI."

[Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

## Justin Hotard: Formation and Mandate

Hotard's background was more specific than the draft's description suggested. Nokia's appointment release said he was born in 1974, held a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and an MBA from MIT Sloan, and had spent his career moving through systems engineering, product management, corporate development and general management roles at Motorola, Symbol Technologies, NCR, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Intel. At Intel he ran the Data Center & AI Group. At HPE his final role was Executive Vice President and General Manager of High Performance Computing, AI & Labs. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

That background mattered because Nokia had already decided, before Hotard's arrival, to spend more aggressively behind data-centre networking. In the Q4 2024 report Lundmark said Nokia would invest up to an additional EUR 100 million of annual operating expense to pursue EUR 1 billion of incremental data-centre-networking revenue by 2028. Hotard was therefore not arriving to invent the pivot; he was arriving to operationalise and accelerate it. [Nokia Q4 2024 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-and-full-year-2024/)

## First Weeks in Charge

Hotard's first substantive shareholder communication came with the Q1 2025 interim report on 24 April 2025. He said his early focus was on capital allocation, efficiency and investment in the right growth segments, and he explicitly highlighted hyperscale, enterprise and defence as areas where Nokia could expand. [Nokia Q1 2025 interim report](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/04/24/nokia-corporation-interim-report-for-q1-2025/)

The numbers he inherited were mixed but informative. Group net sales were EUR 4.390 billion. On Nokia's comparable basis, Network Infrastructure grew 11 per cent and Optical Networks 15 per cent, while Mobile Networks grew 2 per cent but was hit by a one-time EUR 120 million contract-settlement charge. Hotard kept the full-year comparable operating-profit guide at EUR 1.9 billion to EUR 2.4 billion. The first verdict on his opening quarter was therefore not that he had changed Nokia's numbers, but that he had inherited an optical-and-routing growth pocket large enough to talk about seriously and still small enough that the legacy carrier base dominated the P&L. [Nokia Q1 2025 interim report](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/04/24/nokia-corporation-interim-report-for-q1-2025/) [Nokia Q1 2025 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2025-04/nokia_slides_2025_q1_fi.pdf)

## Marco Wirén: The Financial Counterweight

Chief Financial Officer Marco Wirén provided continuity across that transition. Nokia's leadership materials described him as a 1966-born Swedish national with a master's degree in business administration from Uppsala University. Before Nokia he had held senior finance and operating roles at NCC, Eltel Networks, SSAB and Wärtsilä, including as CFO of both SSAB and Wärtsilä and later as president of Wärtsilä Energy. At Nokia he also carried the title of Chief Risk Officer. [Marco Wirén bio](https://www.nokia.com/index.php/about-us/company/leadership-and-governance/group-leadership-team/marco-wiren/)

That profile mattered because the Hotard transition was not simply a growth-story rewrite. It sat on top of a live restructuring programme, an acquisition integration, a shareholder-return programme and a balance-sheet reset after the carrier-spending downturn. Wirén was the executive responsible for keeping those moving parts financeable while management raised optical capacity and protected R&D.

## Segment Leadership: The Frozen-Window Version

This was the area where the earlier draft had drifted furthest from the frozen window. At the moment Hotard took office in April 2025, the four major business lines were still led by Federico Guillén in Network Infrastructure, Tommi Uitto in Mobile Networks, Raghav Sahgal in Cloud and Network Services, and Patrik Hammarén in Nokia Technologies, with Hammarén having formally taken the latter role on 22 January 2025. [Patrik Hammarén appointment](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/patrik-hammaren-appointed-as-president-of-nokia-technologies/) [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

That roster changed twice before the frozen snapshot. First, on 16 June 2025 Nokia said Federico Guillén would retire from Nokia on 31 December 2025 and step down as President of Network Infrastructure and from the Group Leadership Team on 30 June 2025. David Heard, former CEO of Infinera and then Nokia's NI Chief Strategic Growth Officer, would take over as President of Network Infrastructure from 1 July 2025. [Group leadership changes, June 2025](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-changes-to-group-leadership-team/)

Second, on 19 November 2025 Nokia reset the operating model entirely. From 1 January 2026, the company said, Mobile Infrastructure would bring together Core Software, Radio Networks and Technology Standards and would be led by Justin Hotard on an interim basis. At the same time, Sahgal moved to Chief Customer Officer and Hammarén continued in the Group Leadership Team as President of Technology Standards. By 13 May 2026 Nokia had also announced Emma Falck as the future President of Mobile Infrastructure, but her start date was 1 September 2026 — after the frozen snapshot — which meant Hotard was still the interim head of that segment on 23 May 2026. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/) [Emma Falck appointment](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-appoints-emma-falck-as-president-of-mobile-infrastructure-and-member-of-the-group-leadership-team/)

## Board Oversight: From Baldauf to Ihamuotila

The chapter title reflected the first part of the period, not the last. Baldauf absolutely chaired the board through the Hotard recruitment, and her Nokia history made her central to understanding that decision. She had joined Nokia's board in 2018, become chair in 2020, and had earlier served as Executive Vice President and General Manager of Nokia's Networks Business Group in the company's pre-smartphone peak era. [Nokia transition release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-announces-a-leadership-transition---justin-hotard-appointed-as-successor-to-pekka-lundmark/)

But by the frozen snapshot she no longer chaired Nokia. At the 29 April 2025 AGM, shareholders elected Timo Ihamuotila as vice chair and Pernille Erenbjerg to the board, while Baldauf remained chair. At the 9 April 2026 AGM, however, Baldauf was no longer among the elected directors. In the board's post-AGM assembly meeting, Timo Ihamuotila was elected chair and Thomas Saueressig vice chair. [Nokia AGM 2025 decisions](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporations-board-of-directors-assembly-meeting-decisions-and-dividend/) [Nokia AGM 2026 resolutions](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/resolutions-of-nokia-corporations-annual-general-meeting-and-board-of-directors-assembly-meeting-807431/)

The committee structure had also rotated by April 2026. Nokia said Pernille Erenbjerg would chair the Audit Committee; Saueressig the Corporate Governance and Nomination Committee; Thomas Dannenfeldt the Personnel Committee; Kai Öistämö the Technology Committee; and Elizabeth Crain the Strategy Committee. That is the governance architecture that actually sat above Hotard, Heard and Wirén at the frozen date, not the 2025 configuration carried in the earlier draft. [Nokia AGM 2026 resolutions](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/resolutions-of-nokia-corporations-annual-general-meeting-and-board-of-directors-assembly-meeting-807431/)

## What Leadership Meant in Practice

The leadership picture by 23 May 2026 was therefore more dynamic than a static roster implied. Hotard had come in as the AI-and-data-centre chief executive; Heard had replaced Guillén to run the business group most exposed to hyperscaler spending; Hammarén had moved from licensing into a broader standards role inside Mobile Infrastructure; Sahgal had been shifted from stand-alone segment management into customer orchestration; and the board that had hired Hotard had already handed the chair to Ihamuotila. Those changes did not guarantee execution. They did show that Nokia was willing to reshape both its reporting lines and its senior bench quickly once it had committed to the AI-supercycle framing.

chapters.title: Telecom carriers, hyperscaler AI data centres, patent licensees
chapters.body:
Nokia's commercial map by the frozen snapshot date was easier to understand than the old conglomerate narrative implied. The company sold into three very different customer sets: telecom operators buying radio, core and fibre infrastructure; AI and cloud operators buying optical and IP gear; and licensees paying for the use of Nokia's patent estate. The supply chain underneath those relationships was equally hybrid: part proprietary optical technology, part merchant-component ecosystem, and part globally dispersed contract manufacturing. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia supplier list 2024](https://www.nokia.com/sites/default/files/2024-03/nokia-supplier-list-2024.pdf)

## The Carrier Franchise

Carrier customers remained the core revenue base even after the AI pivot. Nokia's own releases before the frozen date showed the breadth of that footprint across multiple regions and product layers. In India, [Reliance Jio](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2022/10/17/nokia-wins-multi-year-deal-with-reliance-jio-india-to-build-one-of-the-largest-5g-networks-in-the-world/) selected Nokia in October 2022 as a major supplier of 5G RAN equipment in a nationwide multi-year deal. In Germany, [Telefónica Germany](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-telefonica-germany-agree-5-year-ran-deal-to-advance-5g-expansion/) extended its 5G RAN relationship for five years in November 2025. In the UK, [Virgin Media O2](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-wins-new-5g-ran-deal-with-virgin-media-o2-to-accelerate-its-mobile-transformation-plan/) selected Nokia in March 2026 for a new multi-year 5G deployment and modernisation programme. And at Mobile World Congress 2026 Nokia disclosed deeper AI-native and Open RAN collaboration with [Deutsche Telekom](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2026/03/02/nokia-and-deutsche-telekom-expand-strategic-collaboration-to-advance-ai-native-and-open-ran-innovation-mwc26/) and an AI-ready 5G network expansion with [TIM Brasil](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2026/03/02/nokia-expands-partnership-with-tim-brasil-to-deliver-next-generation-ai-ready-5g-network-with-nvidia-mwc26/).

Those disclosures supported a narrower and more defensible claim than the earlier draft made. Nokia remained a real Tier-1 carrier supplier across India, continental Europe, the UK and Latin America-linked operator groups. What they did not support was a precise global share estimate, so the old RAN-share shorthand is better understood as inference than filed fact.

## Hyperscalers, AI Cloud and the New Buyer Set

The more novel customer vector was hyperscale and AI infrastructure. Infinera mattered because it imported customer relationships that Nokia's legacy optical business had not built at the same depth. Nokia's public win set before the frozen date made that visible. In December 2024 [Nscale](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-building-ip-network-to-support-ai-workloads-at-nscales-new-sustainable-data-center/) selected Nokia to provide the IP network supporting AI workloads at its new Norway data centre. In May 2025 [CoreSite](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/05/13/nokia-selected-by-coresite-for-routing-based-network-edge-solution-to-support-data-intensive-mission-critical-applications/) chose Nokia for an IP-routing-based edge and core solution across 30 US data centres in 11 markets. Nokia also disclosed that [CoreWeave](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-selected-by-coreweave-to-provide-networking-backbone-behind-hyperscale-ai-cloud/) would deploy Nokia IP and optical platforms across data centres in the US and Europe as part of its hyperscale AI cloud backbone.

The company then used partnerships to widen the go-to-market motion. In September 2025 Nokia and [Supermicro](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-supermicro-partner-to-deliver-integrated-ai-optimized-data-center-networking-solutions/) announced an integrated AI-optimised data-centre networking solution. In May 2026, still inside the frozen window, Nokia launched an [AI Networking Innovation Lab](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-launches-ai-networking-lab-to-drive-co-innovation-with-partners-and-accelerate-next-era-of-ai-native-data-center-networking/) to test and validate large-scale AI data-centre architectures with partners. By Q1 2026 Nokia said AI & Cloud net sales were up 49 per cent year on year and accounted for 8 per cent of group sales. [Nokia Q1 2026 slides](https://www.nokia.com/system/files/2026-04/nokia_slides_2026_q1_fi.pdf)

## Patent Licensees: The Less Visible Customer Base

Nokia Technologies sold something structurally different: legal access to inventions rather than boxes. The official record on named licensees was stronger than the earlier draft suggested, but it needed to be anchored to Nokia's own disclosures. In February 2024 Nokia said it had concluded its smartphone patent renewal cycle and identified agreements with Apple and Samsung in 2023, Huawei in December 2022, and more recent agreements with Honor, OPPO and vivo, plus one additional major smartphone agreement whose counterparty it did not name publicly. [Nokia smartphone renewal cycle](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/inside-information-nokia-concludes-smartphone-patent-license-renewal-cycle/)

The licensing base also extended beyond handsets. In March 2025 Nokia announced a new [patent agreement with Amazon](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/03/31/nokia-and-amazon-sign-patent-agreement/), showing the portfolio's expansion into streaming, devices and broader connected-consumer electronics. By Q4 2025 Nokia was still describing the business in run-rate terms of roughly EUR 1.4 billion of contracted annual net sales. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Supply Chain: Proprietary Optics, Global Assembly

Nokia's annual report and supplier list provided a more concrete view of the supply chain than the draft had. In 2024 Nokia said it did business with around 9,300 suppliers in more than 100 countries and that 80 per cent of supplier spend was concentrated among roughly 400 suppliers. The company's own manufacturing accounted for only 4 per cent of its manufacturing network by site count, excluding the discontinued Submarine Networks business. Nokia said its own factories were in Finland and India, while final-assembly suppliers included Flex, Foxconn, Jabil, Sanmina, Fabrinet and Karel across sites in Canada, China, Hungary, India, Italy, Malaysia, Mexico, Romania and the United States. [Nokia in 2024 Annual Report release](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-has-published-its-nokia-in-2024-annual-report-and-filed-its-annual-report-on-form-20-f-for-2024/) [Nokia supplier list 2024](https://www.nokia.com/sites/default/files/2024-03/nokia-supplier-list-2024.pdf)

That same disclosure makes clear that Nokia's component ecosystem was broad rather than vertically integrated in the Cisco mould. Nokia's 2024 supplier list included Marvell, Intel, MediaTek, Microchip, NXP, Qualcomm, Sanmina, Flex and Hon Hai, among others. It did not identify which silicon went into which product family, but it did support the narrower claim that Nokia depended on a diversified merchant-component base alongside its own software and system integration. [Nokia supplier list 2024](https://www.nokia.com/sites/default/files/2024-03/nokia-supplier-list-2024.pdf)

## Infinera's Optical Manufacturing Edge

Where the portfolio was genuinely more proprietary was optical. Infinera's final 10-K before the Nokia close described the company as a vertically integrated optical-networking supplier using indium phosphide-based photonic integrated circuits, produced with in-house semiconductor capabilities, as a central differentiator in its systems. That mattered because Nokia did not just buy more optical customers; it also bought a deeper manufacturing and design stack in coherent optics. [Infinera 2024 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1138639/000113863925000035/infn-20241228.htm)

The operational consequence was visible in Nokia's own 2026 commentary. The company said it expected higher capital expenditure in 2026 partly because it was investing in additional manufacturing capacity to support the growth outlook in Optical Networks. In other words, the supply chain itself had become a strategic bottleneck worth spending against. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

chapters.title: Where Nokia sits against Ericsson, Cisco, Juniper, Arista, Huawei, broader
chapters.body:
## The Shape of the Battlefield

Nokia's competitive map divided into two overlapping arenas by the frozen window. In radio access and mobile core, the main benchmarks remained Ericsson, Samsung Networks and Huawei. In routing, optical transport and AI-era data-centre fabrics, the reference set shifted to Cisco, Arista and the HPE-owned Juniper portfolio. What changed during 2025 was not the existence of those rivals; it was Nokia's decision to treat the second group as strategically primary. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Ericsson: The Closest Radio Peer

Ericsson remained Nokia's cleanest like-for-like comparison in the traditional telecom-vendor universe: both were Nordic suppliers, both had spent years restructuring around 5G, and both benefited from the reduced role of Huawei in several Western markets. What Nokia had that Ericsson did not was a large, internally owned IP-and-optical platform into which management was now funnelling disproportionate strategic attention. When Nokia described the convergence of IP and optical as a defining advantage in the AI build-out, Ericsson was the example implicitly left outside that frame. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/) [Nokia strategy summary](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-unveils-strategy-to-capture-value-from-ai-supercycle/)

That did not make Ericsson irrelevant. It meant Nokia's competitive stress in radio remained real even as investors increasingly focused on AI-linked infrastructure. Nokia's own disclosures continued to present mobile as a stable but not fast-growing market, with profitability improvement rather than top-line acceleration as the main internal objective for Mobile Infrastructure. [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

## Cisco: The Routing Incumbent

In service-provider routing and adjacent data-centre networking, Cisco remained the incumbent Nokia had to dislodge rather than simply match. Nokia's formal answer to that problem was SR Linux plus optical integration. The company repeatedly said in 2024-2026 disclosures that AI & Cloud customers were driving order intake in both Optical and IP Networks, and it backed that claim with wins such as Nscale, CoreSite and CoreWeave. Nokia's argument was that the buyer increasingly cared about the interaction between the routed fabric and the optical layer underneath it, not just the software stack on the router itself. [Nscale](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-building-ip-network-to-support-ai-workloads-at-nscales-new-sustainable-data-center/) [CoreSite](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/05/13/nokia-selected-by-coresite-for-routing-based-network-edge-solution-to-support-data-intensive-mission-critical-applications/) [CoreWeave](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-selected-by-coreweave-to-provide-networking-backbone-behind-hyperscale-ai-cloud/) [Nokia Q4 2025 report](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-corporation-financial-report-for-q4-2025-and-full-year-2025/)

That claim did not prove Cisco weakness; it clarified Nokia's attack surface. Cisco could still sell the routing layer on incumbency, scale and installed operational comfort. Nokia's route in was to make the IP-over-optical bundle itself the differentiator.

## Juniper, Now Inside HPE

The earlier draft treated Juniper as if it were still only a pending variable. By the frozen window, that was outdated. Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced on 2 July 2025 that it had completed its acquisition of Juniper Networks. For Nokia, that mattered because a historically service-provider-centric routing rival had gained a far larger enterprise and systems-sales parent, potentially increasing the number of channels through which it could pursue AI-networking budgets. [HPE closes Juniper acquisition](https://www.hpe.com/us/en/newsroom/press-release/2025/07/hewlett-packard-enterprise-closes-acquisition-of-juniper-networks-to-offer-industry-leading-comprehensive-cloud-native-ai-driven-portfolio.html)

At the same time, HPE-Juniper was also an integration story of its own, which meant Nokia was not the only company trying to explain a networking portfolio through a new AI-era lens. The distinction was that Nokia had paired its routing push with Infinera's optical layer, whereas HPE paired Juniper with a broader compute-and-enterprise stack.

## Arista: The Data-Centre Specialist

If Cisco was the routing incumbent and Ericsson the radio peer, Arista was the specialist Nokia most directly needed to unsettle inside AI data-centre fabrics. Nokia's own language increasingly acknowledged that the opportunity was not the traditional telco core; it was cloud, AI and hyperscale interconnect. Public wins at Nscale, CoreSite and CoreWeave showed Nokia was at least being invited into that conversation. But those were footholds in a market where Arista's reputation for cloud-scale Ethernet fabrics and operational simplicity was already deeply embedded. [Nscale](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-building-ip-network-to-support-ai-workloads-at-nscales-new-sustainable-data-center/) [CoreSite](https://www.nokia.com/about-us/news/releases/2025/05/13/nokia-selected-by-coresite-for-routing-based-network-edge-solution-to-support-data-intensive-mission-critical-applications/) [CoreWeave](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-selected-by-coreweave-to-provide-networking-backbone-behind-hyperscale-ai-cloud/)

Nokia's answer was not to out-Arista Arista on software minimalism. It was to argue that Arista could not replicate a single-vendor routed-plus-optical stack after Infinera. Whether hyperscalers valued that enough to change procurement behaviour remained the key commercial unknown.

## Huawei: The Constrained Full-Stack Rival

Huawei remained the most complete competitor on paper because it spanned radio, transport, optical and cloud networking. Its constraint was geopolitical, not architectural. In the UK, for example, the government put the removal of Huawei equipment from 5G networks onto a formal timetable ending in 2027. Restrictions of that sort did not create automatic wins for Nokia, but they did narrow the field in some Western markets and help preserve Nokia's relevance in long-cycle operator tenders. [UK government Huawei decision](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/huawei-to-be-removed-from-uk-5g-networks-by-2027) [Huawei legal notices issued](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/huawei-legal-notices-issued)

Outside those markets, the constraint was weaker. That is why Nokia's competitive argument increasingly emphasised "trusted" infrastructure and western-provider status alongside technical claims. The company was not competing against Huawei on identical commercial terms everywhere.

## Nokia's Actual Edge

The most defensible version of Nokia's competitive claim by May 2026 was narrower than the draft's market-hegemony language. Nokia had a real western telecom installed base, a patent-licensing buffer, a growing optical business after Infinera, and enough IP-routing credibility to win early AI-and-cloud deployments. It also had management explicitly targeting 6-8 per cent annual growth in Network Infrastructure through 2028, with 10-12 per cent growth in the combined Optical Networks and IP Networks businesses. [Nokia strategy update](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-announces-new-strategy-evolution-of-its-operating-model-new-long-term-financial-target-strategic-kpis-and-changes-to-its-group-leadership-team/)
